'''Frederick Reif''' (April 24, 1927 – August 11, 2019)<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Obituary: Frederick Reif / Educator, author and researcher at Carnegie Mellon University |url=https://www.post-gazette.com/news/obituaries/2019/08/17/Obituary-Frederick-Reif-Educator-author-researcher-Carnegie-Mellon-University/stories/201908170036 |access-date=2022-06-18 |website=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette |language=en}}</ref> was an American physicist. He was an emeritus professor in physics and psychology at [[Carnegie Mellon University]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Frederick Reif - Obituary |url=https://www.aapt.org/Membership/Frederick_Reif.cfm |access-date=2022-06-18 |website=www.aapt.org}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Reif was born in [[Vienna, Austria]] on April 24, 1927, to Gerschon and Klara Reif and grew up near the [[Prater]]. His father committed suicide after he was forced to close his practice and was not permitted to work. His family left Austria for [[Cuba]] after the [[Kristallnacht]] on the [[MS St. Louis]] and was forced to return to Europe, where his mother, his sister, and himself disembarked in France, living as refugees under German occupation in [[Loudun]] before relocating to [[Limoges]]. In September 1941, his family secured a visa to the [[United States]] and emigrated to [[New York City]] by way of [[Spain]] and [[Portugal]].<ref name=":1" />

Reif completed high school at [[Erasmus Hall High School]] and entered [[Columbia University]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bookshelf {{!}} Columbia College Today |url=https://www.college.columbia.edu/cct/archive/jul_aug09/bookshelf |access-date=2022-06-18 |website=www.college.columbia.edu |archive-date=2022-06-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220614234735/https://www.college.columbia.edu/cct/archive/jul_aug09/bookshelf |url-status=dead }}</ref> but was drafted into the army at age 18. Upon completion of his services, he returned to Columbia to obtain his B.A. in 1948 and moved onto [[Harvard University]] to obtain his doctorate in 1953 under the guidance of [[Edward Mills Purcell]].<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Frederick Reif |url=https://senate.universityofcalifornia.edu/in-memoriam/files/frederick-reif.html |access-date=2022-06-18 |website=senate.universityofcalifornia.edu}}</ref> His thesis was on [[nuclear magnetic resonance]] in [[solid hydrogen]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Remembering Frederick Reif {{!}} UC Berkeley Physics |url=https://physics.berkeley.edu/news-events/news/20190826/remembering-frederick-reif |access-date=2022-06-18 |website=physics.berkeley.edu |archive-date=2022-06-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220625134928/https://physics.berkeley.edu/news-events/news/20190826/remembering-frederick-reif |url-status=dead }}</ref> He joined the faculty of the [[University of Chicago]] in 1953, working with [[Enrico Fermi]] and Lothar Meyer. At Chicago, he focused on the studies of [[superfluid helium]].<ref name=":2" />

He was later hired as a professor at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where he taught from 1960 to 1989.<ref name=":2" /> At Berkeley, he discovered that electrons in liquid helium were attached to microscopic and quantized vortex rings, matching the prediction made by [[Lars Onsager]] and [[Richard Feynman]]. He also discovered gapless superconductivity, which was proposed by [[Alexei Abrikosov (physicist)|Alexei Abrikosov]] and [[Lev Gor'kov]]. His students at Berkeley included [[George W. Rayfield]], [[Jill H. Larkin]], and [[Clifford Surko]].<ref name=":2" />

He then joined the faculty of [[Carnegie Mellon University]] and remained a faculty member until 2000. His research in physics has focused on properties of matter at low temperatures, and he also focused on the physics education and the psychology of learning during the second half of his career.<ref name=":2" />

Reif was known for his research in physics education.<ref name=":1" /> He is the author of popular textbooks such as ''Fundamentals of Thermal and Statistical Physics'' (1965), ''Statistical Physics'' (1967), and ''Understanding Basic Mechanics'' (1995), and co-founded the first interdisciplinary PhD program in physics with [[Robert Karplus]] at Berkeley, The Graduate Group in Science and Mathematics Education, also known informally as SESAME. He also helped write one of the [[Berkeley Physics Course]] textbooks with funding from the [[National Science Foundation]] aimed to improve undergraduate teaching in physics.<ref name=":2" /> For his contributions in the teaching of physics, he received the [[Robert A. Millikan award|Robert A. Millikan Award]] from the [[American Association of Physics Teachers]].<ref name=":1" />

Reif was a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] and the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].<ref name=":1" />

== Personal life ==
Reif died on August 11, 2019, at age 92.<ref name=":2" /> He was a longtime resident of [[Fox Chapel, Pennsylvania]].<ref name=":0" /> His first wife was [[Mildred Dresselhaus]]. He later married Laura Ott and then [[Jill H. Larkin]] Wellman, his former Ph.D. student. His sister Liane Reif-Lehrer, was a biochemist and professor at [[Harvard Medical School]], and his niece is anthropologist [[Erica Lehrer]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lehrer |first=Erica |date=August 21, 2019 |title=Frederick Reif |url=https://physicstoday.scitation.org/do/10.1063/pt.6.4o.20190821a/full |access-date=June 17, 2022 |journal=Physics Today|doi=10.1063/pt.6.4o.20190821a |s2cid=240784423 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>
